Founders budget for AI hiring tools the same way they budget for a project management app: monthly fee, seat count, done. That's the wrong line item, and it's why so many of these tools get bought well and run badly.

The subscription cost is the smallest part of what it actually takes to run one of these tools responsibly. The real cost is time. Someone has to configure it against your actual hiring criteria, not the vendor's defaults. Someone has to check its output against real outcomes on a set schedule, not just at renewal. Someone has to be the name attached to it when a candidate asks why they were screened out, and that person needs real hours in their week to actually answer.

None of that shows up on the vendor's pricing page, and almost no founder adds it to the budget before signing. So the tool gets bought, configured once, and left to run on autopilot for months, because the actual cost of running it right was never on the spreadsheet in the first place.

Before you sign the next AI hiring tool contract, budget the ongoing hours next to the monthly fee, not just the fee. If nobody has time on their calendar for it, you haven't budgeted for the tool. You've budgeted for the demo.

What did your last AI hiring tool actually cost once you counted the time, not just the invoice?

As we study the AI landscape ahead of Anthropic’s IPO, its very interesting to understand where the money goes and who depends on it.

Anthropic’s November 10 filing lists about $901 billion in future spending commitments, mostly for computing power and infrastructure. These span many years; they are not money already spent or the cost of the IPO. 

There is substantial business behind those commitments, too: Anthropic reported $33.2 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026. Revenue, however, is not the same as profit. 

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱-𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀:
→ Chipmakers, cloud providers and data centres.
→ Construction crews, electricians, cooling specialists and power companies.
→ Banks and investment funds financing the expansion. 

The rise of AI ecosystem has created various interdependent economies.

India is part of this, too. Its data-centre sector has nearly $70 billion in investment underway, supporting AI and other digital services,not AI alone. 

If investment across the sector slows sharply, the possible effects include delayed projects, fewer supplier orders and weaker hiring. Lenders and investors could also face losses if the businesses they finance cannot meet their obligations. 

Some financial exposure reaches pension and insurance portfolios through investments in technology companies and infrastructure financing. 

The risk is not equal everywhere: it depends on debt, contract terms and how much each portfolio has invested.

That's why we don't ask you to commit first.

Here's what the two-week program actually looks like:

Day 1–2: We learn how you work. What software you use, how bills get coded, who approves what, where the bottlenecks are. You show us, we take notes.

Day 3–5: We connect to your systems with the access level you choose. Read-only at first if you want. The agent watches and learns your patterns.

Day 6–10: It starts doing work. Small tasks first—coding transactions, drafting follow-up emails, flagging exceptions. We tune it every day based on what you see.

Day 11–14: Full daily workflow. You review its work each morning. We adjust anything that's off.

At the end: a scorecard of what it handled, how long each task took, and a firm quote.

No surprises. No contract until you've seen it work in your business.

A professional video is not automatically transformative content.

The distance between the two is often the experience of your production partner: and the questions you ask before signing.

A strong reel is only a starting point. Your partner should show relevant work, explain who will do the work, protect your information, and make ownership clear.

Before hiring a film production company, ask:

1. What is your specific expertise, and can you show recent work matching our technical requirements?
Ask for work from the last 12 months that reflects your project’s complexity.

2. Who will actually be on my project, and what is their direct experience?
This can expose the bait-and-switch where the senior creative who pitched you disappears after the contract.

3. How do you use AI and modern technology while protecting data privacy, ownership, and creative integrity?
Understand which tools may be used, how information is handled, and where human judgment leads.

4. What is your production process, and how do you manage milestones and revisions?
Clarify pre-production, production, post-production, review, delivery, and the number of revision rounds included.

5. Who owns the raw footage and final deliverables, and what are the usage rights?
Define raw versus edited files, time limits, and geographic or medium restrictions.

Companies rarely design their global employment setup.
 
It accumulates.
 
This spring we ran two roundtables with People Directors and Heads of HR from companies employing in anywhere from 5 to 30+ countries. Almost everyone told the same story. An EOR in one country. Contractors plugging gaps in another. A local lawyer somewhere else. Contracts sitting on someone’s desktop.
 
Nobody planned it. They grew into it.
 
The words they used said a lot: fragile, convoluted, “building the tracks in front of the train.”
 
Four themes kept coming up:
 
Compliance is hope-based. Changes get flagged late by providers, or by an employee first. “That’s a bit cringe,” as one People Lead put it.

The vendor patchwork. Two or three providers is normal. One team in Turkey found their global provider had put them “in contact with contact with contact.”

AI hits a ceiling. It’s fine for the notice period in Spain. On anything with real consequences, it’s confidently wrong.

The standardisation dance. What’s fair in one country isn’t fair in another, and the EU Pay Transparency Directive is forcing the issue.
 
The honest bit: nobody claimed to have it sorted. Most were somewhere between “patchwork” and “coordinated.”
 
A lot of this goes back to one decision, usually made under pressure: how do we hire in this new country? EOR, entity or contractor. Pick quickly and you can end up living with it for years.
 
That’s what we’re covering tomorrow (Wed 18 Nov) at 2pm UK, fully virtual: Choosing the right global hiring model.

General Motors is aiming for 20% more automation across its North American factories by 2028.

The part getting less attention: GM is building its own robots in Kokomo, Indiana, and scoring suppliers on their automation plans when awarding new contracts.

Automation expectations are now moving down the supply chain.

What that means for hiring:

➡️ Demand grows for robotics, controls, maintenance, and AI-adjacent technicians
➡️ Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers will need those same skills to stay competitive for contracts
➡️ The talent pool is small, and OEMs and suppliers will be fishing in the same pond
➡️ Automation eases line labor shortages, but creates new shortages in specialized roles

GM says it has about 100 roboticists, AI engineers, and hardware specialists on this effort already. Suppliers don’t have that head start.

Manufacturers must start to map their future skill needs now to hire ahead of the curve. If not, they'll be recruiting reactively against a tighter market.

Is your hiring plan built for the plant you have today or the one you’ll need in 2028?

Workday’s defense in the biggest AI hiring case in the country comes down to one idea:

Our customers make the hiring decisions.

Last week, Workday asked the court to break up the age-discrimination group in Mobley v. Workday, which now includes more than 15,000 applicants. 

Its argument is that the plaintiffs cannot show Workday made hiring decisions for its customers. 

Workday denies the claims, and nothing has been decided on the merits.

If the vendor didn’t make the decision, the employer did.

The contracts tend to agree. Lawyers call it a liability squeeze. 

Courts are expanding what vendors can be held accountable for, while the agreements cap the vendor’s exposure and leave the risk with the customer.

The law stayed put: Title VII, the ADA and the ADEA still apply, and states are adding rules of their own.

So when a screening outcome is challenged, the sequence is predictable.

The vendor points to your configuration.

The contract points to you.

The plaintiff’s attorney asks for your file.

Organizations that hold up have written down how HR keeps ultimate oversight of every decision the tool touches:

Ownership. Every AI screening feature has a named HR owner, and nothing switches on without that person’s approval.

Validation. Before go-live, the tool is tested against your actual roles and job-related criteria, and the results are kept.

Change control. Every configuration change, knockout question and rule exception goes through HR review, with a record of who approved it and why.

Human decision point. A person reviews before any rejection goes out, and that review is logged.

Monitoring. Before a selection is made on any job posting, selection rates by sex, race and age are reviewed at each stage. 

Reviews continue until enough data shows the tool performs in compliance, and responses are documented.

Contract rights. The vendor agreement guarantees your access to the data, audit rights and documentation to run all of the above.

As an owner-side application lead for HR systems in a regulated environment, I asked these questions before anything was built, to keep issues like this from arising:

What decision is this tool actually making?

Who owns that decision?

What happens when a case doesn’t fit the rule?

What will we need to produce if someone challenges the outcome?

The answers became the requirements, and the requirements shaped the design.

Here is what concerns me most.

HR teams are being cut to the bone. 

Meanwhile, the vendors are planning next year’s conference, where the newest bells and whistles will shine on stage.

Every feature that goes live without an HR owner is a decision HR assumed someone else would answer for.

It is time to take that ownership back.

HR designs the program, sets the rules and answers for the outcome. 

The technology carries out what HR decided.

Write the process before the system goes live, with compliance in mind.

I joined Daniel Ostrovsky, Jeremy Davis and Nick Taylor on the XtremeJS 2026 panel this week to talk about AI, JavaScript, and where web development is headed.

One conversation stood out - the scope of jobs AI is condensing right now.

I'm speaking to private equity general partners managing a $10 billion fund, and they're saying it's easier for me to connect to a private portfolio company HubSpot and run some MCP queries in 30 minutes versus hiring an analyst or working with a company and doing interviews and hiring them and contract and decks - I can do my job in an hour on a Saturday afternoon versus working with a third party.

We're seeing CMOs sending detailed mocks with "integrate that by adhering to the best performance and accessibility and security and speed and SEO, but this is what it should look like" - saving that five week mockups and wireframes process that's been standard for 15 years.

It's the entire field of software product engineering - frontend developers, mobile developers, backend, DBAs - and beyond that, virtually every office job: CPAs, legal, marketers, copywriters, designers.

The top 5%, maybe top 10% of every field are going to survive and stay relevant. Everyone else is going to have a pretty rough time.

We posted a COO job. The best applicant had run Canada's largest janitorial company.
⠀
Yesterday I said Mathias and I were building AI tools for small businesses.
⠀
Here's how that turned into cleaning.
⠀
At Portico, we built AI systems for different industries. A flooring company. A longevity clinic.
⠀
Then we pivoted to an AI call center. That one worked.
⠀
So we went looking for a COO.
⠀
Neil applied.
⠀
Of everyone I interviewed, he knew the most, by far.
⠀
He'd hired cleaning companies as a property manager. Then he ran Canada's largest one.
⠀
He looked at what we were building and told us the bigger opportunity was somewhere else.
⠀
Cleaning.
⠀
Not because it's exciting. Because he'd sat on both sides of the contract, and he knew what breaks.
⠀
The property manager can't see the work. The cleaning company can't prove it.
⠀
So we listened.
⠀
3 things I learned from hiring him:
⠀
1. Post the job anyway. The best person might not be in your network yet.
2. Hire someone who has lived your customer's problem, from both sides.
3. When that person says the bigger opportunity is somewhere else, listen.
⠀
Neil is our COO and co-founder now.
⠀
Founders: did your best hire come from a job post or from your network? 👇
⠀
